topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited to public health education contexts; findings on faculty development approaches may transfer to other disciplines but sector-specific barriers and solutions are not yet clear from the snippet provided.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI adoption is addressable through structured professional development — design programs that move educators from skepticism to confidence, not just awareness.
Position AI literacy training for educators as foundational; staff capability directly enables student capability in public health roles.
Tailor faculty development to discipline-specific concerns and use cases in public health rather than generic AI training.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on middle school education context; applicability to adult workplace AI literacy development and organisational settings requires adaptation. Geographic scope and specific jurisdictions not clear from title and snippet.
takeaways: AI literacy for non-specialists works best when integrated into existing digital literacy frameworks rather than taught as a standalone subject — consider embedding AI competencies into your organisation's broader digital upskilling programs.

A holistic approach to AI competencies (combining conceptual understanding, practical skills, and critical thinking) is more effective than technical training alone — design programs that build foundational AI literacy across mixed ability levels, not just for technical roles.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European public health context; findings on digital competencies may apply more broadly but public health system structures and regulatory environments differ across regions including Australia.
takeaways: Identify which digital competencies are most critical for your health sector workforce by consulting the framework's competency clusters — this helps prioritise training investments rather than attempting blanket upskilling.
Use the framework's role-specific competency mapping to tailor AI literacy programmes to different job levels (clinical, administrative, leadership) rather than one-size-fits-all approaches.

Consider how European regulatory and system contexts may differ from Australian public health structures; adapt the framework to align with local compliance requirements and organisational priorities before implementation.

articles.title: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey research typically draws on global client work and surveys, but findings may skew toward large enterprises and developed economies. Applicability to smaller Australian organisations or specific sectors may vary.
takeaways: Prioritise identifying which roles will be augmented vs. displaced by gen AI in your organisation, then design targeted upskilling pathways for employees in augmented roles rather than attempting broad-brush reskilling.
Integrate gen AI literacy into foundational training programmes now — employees need to understand AI's capabilities and limitations before learning role-specific AI tools.

Create clear career progression frameworks showing how employees can move into higher-value roles post-upskilling, as this significantly improves engagement and reduces turnover during organisational AI transitions.

articles.title: Development and influencing factors of artificial intelligence literacy and computational thinking in Chinese university students - Nature
articles.snippet: Development and influencing factors of artificial intelligence literacy and computational thinking in Chinese university students  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited to Chinese university students; findings may not generalise to other educational contexts, workforce settings, or countries with different AI curricula and educational systems. Results reflect a specific higher education landscape.
takeaways: Identify which influencing factors (e.g. prior programming experience, teaching methods, institutional support) most strongly predict AI literacy gains in your organisation, then prioritise those in your capability development program.
Use the study's framework for measuring AI literacy and computational thinking to benchmark your workforce's current capability level and design targeted interventions around identified gaps.

Consider how organisational factors analogous to university-level influences—such as access to hands-on AI projects, quality of instruction, and integration with existing workflows—shape employee AI capability development in your workplace.

articles.title: Fostering AI literacy in pre-service teachers: impact of a training intervention on awareness, attitude and trust in AI - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Fostering AI literacy in pre-service teachers: impact of a training intervention on awareness, attitude and trust in AI  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited to pre-service teacher population; findings may not generalise to experienced educators or non-teaching professions. Geographic scope unclear from title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Structured training interventions can measurably improve teachers' AI awareness, attitude, and trust — consider designing similar foundational modules for your organisation's upskilling programs.

Pre-service teacher training is a strategic intervention point; if you work with educational institutions or early-career cohorts, embedding AI literacy into induction or onboarding may be more effective than ad-hoc later training.

The study's focus on attitude and trust alongside awareness suggests that building confidence and positive perception of AI tools is as important as conveying knowledge — balance technical content with reassurance and practical examples.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability cannot be assessed without access to the full article; the snippet provides only the title and source. The finding of a 'double-edged' effect suggests context-dependent outcomes, but geographic scope, sample characteristics, and methodological details are unknown.
takeaways: AI adoption in organisations may simultaneously enhance and inhibit employee creativity depending on implementation approach — consider whether your AI tools are designed to augment human creativity or replace creative thinking.

When introducing AI, explicitly assess potential negative pathways (e.g., over-reliance, skill deskilling, or reduced autonomy) alongside expected benefits to manage unintended consequences on creative output.

articles.title: Corporate sustainability and artificial intelligence-enabled workforce transformation: a dual-pathway model of employee capability, empowerment, anxiety, and job insecurity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Corporate sustainability and artificial intelligence-enabled workforce transformation: a dual-pathway model of employee capability, empowerment, anxiety, and job insecurity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear from title and snippet alone; likely limited by unstated sample characteristics, geographic scope, and sector focus. A full-text review would be needed to assess sample size, diversity, and methodological robustness.
takeaways: AI-enabled transformation can trigger competing psychological outcomes — increased capability and empowerment alongside anxiety and job insecurity — requiring dual-pathway interventions that address both opportunity and threat simultaneously.

Employee empowerment and anxiety appear to operate through separate mechanisms during AI adoption; leaders should not assume that capability-building alone will reduce insecurity, and may need targeted communication and support strategies addressing job security concerns independently.

Linking AI transformation explicitly to corporate sustainability goals may help frame capability development as purposeful and protective, rather than purely efficiency-driven, potentially moderating anxiety and job insecurity among affected staff.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited clarity from title and snippet alone; likely assumes paternalistic leadership contexts (more common in certain Asian cultures) which may not generalise to Australia's more egalitarian workplace norms.
takeaways: Cultivate psychological ownership of AI tools among employees — when staff feel genuine stake in how AI is implemented and shaped for their roles, they collaborate more effectively with it rather than resist adoption.

Frame AI integration as a crafting opportunity: allow employees to customise and adapt AI tools to their workflows rather than imposing one-size-fits-all solutions, which increases buy-in and practical engagement.

Consider how leadership style influences AI adoption outcomes — paternalistic approaches may work in some contexts but merit testing against Australia's more participative leadership expectations to see where psychological ownership strategies work best.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear without access to full methodology; likely limited by unspecified geographic scope and sample characteristics. Findings on psychological safety and ethical leadership pathways are theoretically sound but depend on study design and sample composition.
takeaways: AI adoption without intentional focus on psychological safety and ethical leadership creates mental health risks for employees — prioritise creating a psychologically safe environment before and during AI implementation, where staff feel safe raising concerns about AI systems.

Ethical leadership becomes critical during AI transitions — leaders must visibly model responsible AI use, acknowledge limitations and risks, and demonstrate genuine commitment to employee wellbeing rather than efficiency gains alone, to buffer against depression and disengagement.

Monitor employee mental health as a key implementation metric alongside technical adoption metrics; depression and low psychological safety may indicate implementation is proceeding too fast or without adequate stakeholder input.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Scope unclear from snippet alone; generalisability depends on sample composition, industry sectors studied, and geographic locations, which are not evident from the title and snippet provided.
takeaways: AI adoption can trigger distinct psychological responses in employees—some may approach opportunities to engage with AI tools (upskilling, exploring new capabilities) while others may avoid them; managers should assess individual differences in approach-avoidance orientation when rolling out AI and tailor support accordingly.

Job crafting (how employees reshape their roles to increase meaning or reduce demands) is a key mechanism through which employees adapt to AI; creating psychological safety and clear pathways for task redesign may help employees proactively craft roles that complement rather than conflict with AI systems.

Understanding whether employees are approach- or avoidance-oriented toward AI can inform targeted interventions—those with avoidance tendencies may benefit from structured, low-stakes AI training and reassurance about job security, while those approach-oriented may thrive with autonomy to experiment.

articles.title: The mental health implications of artificial intelligence adoption: the crucial role of self-efficacy - Nature
articles.snippet: The mental health implications of artificial intelligence adoption: the crucial role of self-efficacy  Nature
articles.generalisability: Cannot be fully assessed from title and snippet alone; generalisability depends on study design, sample characteristics, and geographic scope, which are not evident from the information provided.
takeaways: Self-efficacy with AI tools appears to be a protective factor for employee mental health during AI adoption — consider assessing and building AI confidence as part of mental wellbeing support, not just technical training.

Organisations should design AI adoption programmes that explicitly strengthen employees' sense of capability and control, as perceived competence may buffer against anxiety and stress responses to technological change.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte's perspective based on consulting experience, likely drawing on client work across multiple sectors, but specific sample details and geographic scope are not provided in the snippet.
takeaways: Move from a technical 'adoption' mindset to a behavioural 'adaptation' framework—this reframes AI implementation as fundamentally about changing how people work, not just deploying technology.
Design change initiatives that explicitly target the human behaviours required for effective AI use, rather than assuming employees will naturally adjust once tools are introduced.
Consider what new workflows, decision-making patterns, and collaboration styles your team needs to develop alongside AI tools, and build structured interventions to support these shifts.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition and geographic scope not evident from title/snippet. The theoretical framework (approach-avoidance motivation) is applicable across contexts, but empirical findings may be limited by study design, sample characteristics, and sector representation.
takeaways: Monitor whether AI adoption is triggering avoidance behaviours (e.g., withdrawal, resistance) versus approach behaviours (e.g., upskilling, role redesign) in your workforce — the same AI implementation can prompt opposite responses depending on how employees perceive threat versus opportunity.

Design AI adoption initiatives to emphasise growth and autonomy rather than job displacement risk; employees who see AI as enabling new work crafting opportunities (expanding responsibilities, learning new skills) are more likely to engage constructively than those who frame it defensively.

Tailor change messaging and support by employee segment — some staff will naturally approach AI adoption as job-crafting opportunity, while others need explicit reassurance, training, and visible examples of role redesign before they shift from avoidance to engagement.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG analysis draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific case studies and sample composition are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a people-first change initiative rather than a purely technical rollout — prioritise workforce upskilling, role redesign, and capability development alongside technology implementation.
Identify and address specific behaviour changes required at different organisational levels (frontline, management, leadership) to embed AI into daily workflows and decision-making.
Use early wins and role-modelling from leaders and high-performing teams to shift mindsets and overcome resistance to AI-enabled ways of working.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without specified empirical data or sample. Insights may reflect US academic and business context primarily.
takeaways: Identify specific work processes in your organisation where AI adoption is reshaping roles, then proactively communicate these changes to affected teams before implementation to reduce uncertainty and resistance.
Design transition support programmes that help employees build new capabilities alongside AI deployment, rather than treating capability development as separate from change management.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone, but the Nature journal suggests peer-reviewed research. Generalisability depends on sample composition (sector, geography, organisation size) which is not detailed in the provided snippet.
takeaways: AI adoption can increase employee depression when organisations fail to establish psychological safety—prioritise transparent communication, involve staff in AI implementation decisions, and create safe spaces for concerns before and during rollout.

Ethical leadership is critical during AI transitions; leaders must model ethical reasoning about AI use, publicly address fairness and job security concerns, and demonstrate commitment to employee wellbeing alongside productivity gains.
Monitor mental health and engagement metrics during AI adoption as leading indicators of implementation success, particularly among staff whose roles are most affected by automation.

articles.title: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: From adoption to impact: Three horizons of AI transformation  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across sectors and geographies, but specific case studies and client contexts are not detailed in the snippet. Findings may reflect practices of larger organisations with greater resources.
takeaways: Map your organisation's AI adoption journey across three distinct horizons (e.g. foundational, scaling, and transformational) to identify where behaviour change interventions are most needed and what support each stage requires.

Recognise that moving from AI adoption to measurable business impact requires deliberate change management — not just technology deployment — meaning you should embed capability-building and organisational redesign alongside AI implementation.

Tailor adoption strategies to each horizon: early stages need cultural shifts and new ways of working, while later stages require leadership alignment and sustained commitment to realise transformational outcomes.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: The science of why friendships keep us healthy - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: The science of why friendships keep us healthy  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: High — draws on established psychological research across diverse populations, though specific studies may be Western-skewed.
takeaways: Strong friendships are linked to measurable health benefits (lower blood pressure, reduced stress hormones, stronger immune function) — social connection literally rewires your biology.
The quality of friendships matters far more than quantity; a few close, genuine relationships outperform large shallow networks for health outcomes.
Social isolation carries health risks comparable to smoking or obesity, making loneliness a legitimate public health concern that deserves as much attention as physical risk factors.

articles.title: Personality traits in musicians with different types of music performance anxiety - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Personality traits in musicians with different types of music performance anxiety  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — findings apply specifically to musicians and may not generalise to non-musical performance contexts or general populations. Sample details not provided in snippet.
takeaways: Even highly trained musicians experience performance anxiety triggered by different factors (audience, technical demands, etc.), suggesting anxiety isn't simply about skill level but about personality-performance interactions.

Different musicians may need different anxiety management strategies based on their personality profiles rather than one-size-fits-all approaches — counterintuitive since we often assume performance anxiety has universal solutions.

The link between personality and specific anxiety triggers reveals that how nervous you get depends less on what you're doing and more on who you are — a fun reminder that stage fright isn't just about the stage.

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: High — appears to be based on cross-cultural data examining personality-music relationships across multiple countries.
takeaways: People's taste in music reveals consistent personality patterns worldwide — suggesting music preference is a universal window into how people's minds work, regardless of culture.

The finding flips a common assumption: rather than music taste being purely shaped by local culture and upbringing, there are deep personality universals that transcend geography and predict what we enjoy listening to.

This is the kind of quirky cross-cultural pattern that reveals how human psychology has genuine 'wiring' beneath all our cultural differences — your personality might predict your Spotify playlist better than your passport.

articles.title: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026 - Wiley & Sons
articles.snippet: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026  Wiley & Sons
articles.generalisability: Scope unclear from snippet alone, but likely synthesises psychological research across studies from multiple countries; generalisability depends on underlying research diversity.
takeaways: True crime isn't just morbid curiosity — psychologists identify genuine psychological needs it satisfies, from sense-making during uncertainty to safe exploration of threat scenarios.
The appeal cuts across demographics in surprising ways; understanding why people are drawn to true crime reveals something unexpected about how humans process fear, control, and justice.
True crime consumption can serve as a form of psychological 'rehearsal' — people aren't just entertained, they're unconsciously problem-solving real-world safety concerns.

articles.title: How dogs think - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: How dogs think  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Moderate — synthesises existing research on canine cognition, but specific studies may vary in sample size and methodology; applicability depends on dog breed, age, and individual differences.
takeaways: Dogs process social cues from humans with remarkable sophistication — they read facial expressions, tone of voice, and body language in ways that rival some primates, making them uniquely attuned to our emotional states.

Contrary to the 'pack hierarchy' myth, dogs don't organise themselves into rigid dominance hierarchies like wolves; they're far more flexible and pragmatic problem-solvers than popular dog training folklore suggests.

Dogs live largely in the present moment and struggle with delayed gratification compared to humans, but excel at learning cause-and-effect relationships through observation — they're watching us constantly and learning what works.

articles.title: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors? - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How good is the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator for predicting leadership-related behaviors?  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — reviews published research on MBTI validity, but findings depend on quality and diversity of underlying studies; MBTI's predictive power may vary across cultural contexts and organisational settings.
takeaways: Despite its massive popularity in corporate settings, MBTI has surprisingly weak empirical support for predicting actual leadership behaviours — a gap between myth and science that reveals how much we want personality type systems to work.

The allure of MBTI for leaders may be more about the compelling narrative it creates (clear types, self-insight) than its actual predictive accuracy, illustrating how humans are drawn to neat categorisation even when evidence suggests messier reality.

This mismatch between MBTI's cultural dominance and its limited validity is a fascinating case study in how pseudoscience gains traction in organisations when the alternative — admitting personality is complex and unpredictable — feels less satisfying.

articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026  PwC

takeaways: Identify specific workforce concerns about psychological safety (e.g., job security, speaking up, inclusion) from PwC's data to benchmark your organisation's safety culture and prioritise interventions most relevant to your team's expressed fears.

Use PwC's regional and demographic breakdowns to segment your workforce and tailor psychological safety initiatives — different employee groups may have distinct concerns requiring differentiated approaches to foster trust and open communication.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — findings depend on the study's sample characteristics (sector, geography, organisation size), which are not detailed in the snippet. The mechanism linking AI adoption to depression via psychological safety erosion may generalise across knowledge-work settings, but context-specific factors (implementation approach, leadership quality, industry) will influence outcomes.
takeaways: AI adoption can inadvertently damage psychological safety if employees fear redundancy, lack transparency about AI's role, or feel excluded from decisions—actively communicate AI's purpose, involve teams in implementation, and create forums where concerns can be raised without penalty.

Ethical leadership during AI transition is critical to protecting mental wellbeing; leaders should model transparency about AI limitations, acknowledge job-redesign concerns openly, and demonstrate commitment to employee welfare alongside efficiency gains.
Monitor psychological safety metrics (e.g. team surveys on speaking up, reporting concerns) before, during, and after AI rollouts as an early warning system for unintended mental health impacts.

articles.title: What Sycophantic AI Can Cost Your Organization - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: What Sycophantic AI Can Cost Your Organization  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Conceptual discussion applicable across organisational contexts, though specific examples and case studies are likely US-centric. Principles of psychological safety and AI alignment are broadly relevant to Australian organisations.
takeaways: Sycophantic AI systems that tell users what they want to hear rather than providing honest feedback can erode psychological safety by discouraging critical thinking and honest dialogue — organisations should audit their AI tools for this tendency and establish norms that value dissent and challenge.

Leaders need to actively model and reinforce that disagreement with AI recommendations is valued, not punished, to counteract the risk that employees defer uncritically to AI outputs and suppress their own judgement or concerns.

Implement review processes where AI-generated recommendations are explicitly questioned and tested by diverse team members before implementation, converting 'sycophantic agreement' into an opportunity to strengthen psychological safety through structured debate.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Limited — BCG practitioner report without disclosed sample details, methodology, or geographic scope. Findings likely reflect patterns from BCG's client base but generalisability to Australian organisations unclear.
takeaways: Psychological safety can reduce barriers that prevent certain employees (e.g. underrepresented groups) from contributing fully, creating more equitable participation in meetings and decision-making.
Leaders should audit whether their team's psychological safety is genuinely inclusive or only benefits already-confident voices; unequal safety for different employee groups undermines equity goals.
Practical levers: establish explicit norms against interruption, invite quiet team members to contribute, and model admitting mistakes to signal that the playing field is genuinely level.

articles.title: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024 - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-focused findings — may not fully reflect Australian workplace dynamics, employment law, or organisational structures. Generalisability limited by potential sampling bias toward APA members and US-based organisations.
takeaways: Identify specific workplace conditions (e.g., manager responsiveness to concerns, permission to speak up without fear of retaliation) that foster psychological safety, then audit your team against these benchmarks to pinpoint gaps.
Use findings to build a business case for psychological safety initiatives with leadership by linking it to retention, engagement, and performance outcomes documented in the 2024 data.

Assess whether your current feedback and speaking-up mechanisms (e.g., anonymous surveys, team meetings, 1-on-1s) actually enable people to voice concerns without career risk — and redesign if they don't.

articles.title: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey analysis based on their client work and broader industry research, but specific implementation details and outcomes may vary significantly by organisational context, sector, and existing capability maturity.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as expanding employee agency rather than automation threat — positioning people as 'superagents' who leverage AI tools can reduce anxiety and increase psychological safety around new technologies.

Create structured opportunities for employees to experiment with AI in their roles before full-scale rollout; psychological safety requires low-stakes learning environments where mistakes with AI tools are treated as development opportunities, not failures.

Address power dynamics explicitly — ensure AI deployment decisions include frontline employee input and transparency about how AI will augment (not replace) their work; this transparency builds trust and reduces the fear that fuels resistance.
